newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lebanese premier accuses Arafat of rocket attack.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese premier accuses Arafat of rocket attack.

text.p: Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri on Monday accused forces loyal to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat of firing rockets from Lebanese soil which injured a woman in northern Israel on Friday.
"It appears that these were Arafat's people who launched those rockets," Hariri told the French daily Le Monde in a telephone interview, but without offering evidence to support the allegation.
Hizbollah guerrillas, fighting to drive Israeli troops from their south Lebanon occupation zone, had denied firing the rockets, and Hariri said he believed them.
"I am certain that this was not Hizbollah...What is certain is that Hizbollah always claims responsibility for its operations," he told the newspaper.
Israel retaliated for the rocket attack with air attacks on southern Lebanese bases belonging to Hizbollah and a radical Palestinian faction.

Hariri also criticised comments Arafat made after last week's Islamic militant suicide bombing of an Israeli market, which killed 13 people as well as two bombers and threw the Middle East peace process into crisis.
Hariri said Arafat had publicly accepted the word of Israeli intelligence in blaming unspecified foreigners for the attack, and that this explained why Israel was attacking Lebanon.
"He takes his information from the Israelis even though he knows it to be false," Hariri said.

"Mr Arafat well knows that Lebanon has endured much and continues to do so to defend the Palestinian cause. The Israelis hold him responsible for their safety. He responds that they (the suicide bombers) came from abroad," Hariri said.
Hariri did not say where he himself believed the bombers had come from.

Arafat made his comment to argue that sanctions imposed by Israel on Palestinian areas after the bombing were misplaced, and to counter charges from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that he had failed to crack down on milkitants.
Netanyahu said on Sunday there was a "growing indication" that the Palestinian Islamic resistance group Hamas was behind the July 30 attack, the deadliest in Israel for over a year.
The French Foreign Ministry said on Monday that it was increasingly concerned about the violence in southern Lebanon.

It said a five-nation monitoring group set up after cross-border violence between Israel and Lebanon in April 1996 had opened talks in the Lebanese town of Naqoura on Sunday in an effort to calm tensions.
The talks went on through the night and were continuing on Monday, a ministry spokesman said.
The monitoring group comprises representatives of France, the United States, Syria, Lebanon and Israel.
